newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major faces more disunity in ranks.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major faces more disunity in ranks.

text.p: A right-wing former cabinet minister fanned further disunity within Britain's ruling Conservatives on Monday when he publicly hesitated to urge voters to back the party at the next general election.

John Redwood, who last year challenged Prime Minister John Major for the party leadership, was asked in a television interview whether people should vote Conservative or for businessman Sir James Goldsmith's fledgling Referendum Party.

"Well, I think you have to ask me that nearer the time when we see what the manifestoes are of the major parties and what the views of the different candidates are," he told a BBC television current affairs programme.
Redwood later, when pressed, added: "Of course I will answer. Vote for the Conservative Party."

His lukewarm endorsement came on the eve of the annual Conservative conference in the southern resort of Bournemouth which Major hopes to use as the springboard for a victory in the general election which he must call by next May.
It added to the woes of the party, which is suffering from renewed allegations of sleaze, and is trailing the opposition Labour Party by over 20 points in the opinion polls.
At the weekend, Major's hopes suffered a fresh blow when Lord McAlpine, a former Conservative Party treasurer, announced he was joining Goldsmith's new party and would chair its annual conference.
Goldsmith's party is calling for a referendum on Britain's future relations with the European Union.

By contrast, Major has said he would call a plebiscite only if, after the next election, he recommended that Britain should join the planned single European currency, an issue on which his party is deeply split.

Arriving for the conference late on Monday, Major responded tetchily to questions on Redwood, seen by many observers as a likely standard bearer of the right in a battle for the leadership should Major lose the election and then retire.
"John Redwood is a Conservative member of parliament. He has made it perfectly clear he is working for a Conservative victory at the next election," he said.

Party chairman Brian Mawhinney derided Goldsmith's party as "a well financed single issue group" and said to compare it with the Conservative Party which has ruled Britain for 17 years was like comparing chalk with cheese.
But sniping from the right on the question of Europe looked set to frustrate Major's attempt to present the party as united and determined this week.

In an interview in the Times on Monday, former party chairman Lord Norman Tebbit attacked Major's wait-and-see position on the single currency, saying electors were entitled to know at the election where the party stood.
"You cannot lead from a position of saying 'I have not made up my mind'," Tebbit, a member of the wing of the party which opposes closer integration with Europe, said.

The other problem facing Major is how to end the party's reputation for sleaze, which has been promoted by the case of former minister Neil Hamilton who has admitted taking 10,000 pounds ($15,000) from political lobbyist Ian Greer.
Hamilton has denied Greer paid him money to ask questions in parliament, but Major has promised full government cooperation with a parliamentary inquiry into his case.
